note: Compared PDF p.2 Theorem 1 with the Lean statement; the 'original' transcription matches the PDF. Hypotheses (nonzero, three pairwise IsCoprime, a+b+c=0, arbitrary field) and the disjunctive conclusion match. Differences are packaging only: extra [DecidableEq k] instance, natDegree instead of degree (a,b,c and radical(abc) are all nonzero so they agree), and Mathlib's radical (product of normalized = monic prime factors) which is Definition 1.

Compared PDF p.3 Theorem 2; transcription matches. All hypotheses present, none added: p,q,r>=1 in N, not ringChar | p,q,r (in char 0 this is p,q,r != 0, vacuous, as the prose intends), 1/p+1/q+1/r<=1 cast to Q so no N-division pitfall, u,v,w nonzero embedded via Polynomial.C. 'Constants' is rendered natDegree = 0, equivalent to lying in k; a,b,c nonzero so no zero-polynomial issue.

Compared PDF p.3 Corollary 1; transcription matches. n>=3, not ringChar k | n, nonzero, pairwise coprime, a^n+b^n=c^n all present with no extra hypotheses; conclusion natDegree = 0 for each is 'constant'. No differences beyond n being a natural number rather than an integer (n>=3 anyway).

Compared PDF p.3 Theorem 3 (and the paper's own Lean on p.11); transcription matches. char != 2,3 is rendered ringChar k != 2 and != 3, equivalent to the paper's 'not ringChar k | 6' since ringChar is 0 or prime. f,g range over all of RatFunc k with no extra hypotheses, and 'constant in k' is exists c, f = RatFunc.C c, the correct notion for rational functions.

Compared PDF p.4 Theorem 4; transcription matches. deg(f^3-g^2) >= deg(f)/2 + 1 is multiplied by 2 to f.natDegree + 2 <= 2*(f^3-g^2).natDegree, an exact equivalence in N with no truncation. Non-constant is 0 < natDegree for both f and g; f^3 != g^2 makes the difference nonzero so natDegree = degree; [CharZero k] is characteristic zero. No extra hypotheses.

Compared PDF p.4 Lemma 1; transcription matches. '/' is Polynomial Euclidean division, which is the exact quotient here because radical a divides a, so a / radical a is the prose a/rad(a) (same as the paper's divRadical). Only difference is the extra [DecidableEq k] instance; the field k is implicit in the prose and arbitrary in Lean.

Compared PDF p.4 Lemma 2 with Definition 2 (W(a,b)=ab'-a'b); transcription matches. Wronskian is unfolded literally as a*derivative b - derivative a*b in a commutative ring with true subtraction; b is arbitrary (may be zero) as in the prose; only a != 0 is assumed. Division is exact as in Lemma 1; only extra is [DecidableEq k].

Compared PDF p.7 Lemma 3; transcription matches. 'degree >= 1' is 1 <= natDegree, which already forces a != 0, so natDegree and degree agree and the zero-polynomial convention (Mathlib radical 0 = 1) never comes into play. Conclusion 1 <= (radical a).natDegree is the same claim; only extra is [DecidableEq k].

Compared PDF p.11 Theorem 5; transcription matches. Characteristic zero is [CharZero k], a,b,c nonzero with a+b+c=0 and no coprimality, 'a,b,c in k' is all three natDegree = 0, and the bound is the same asymmetric deg rad(a) + deg rad(b) + deg(c) (c without radical, exactly as printed). Differences are packaging only: [DecidableEq k] and natDegree for nonzero polynomials.

Compared Appendix 2 Task 3 definition (divisors add up to more than 2n) with Mathlib Nat.Abundant (n < sum of properDivisors). The Lean iff bridges them for all n in N; at n=0 both sides are false (Nat.divisors 0 = empty), so no edge-case gap. Differences: paper says 'integer n' (negatives/0 not meaningfully covered by the paper); this is a definitional bridge rather than a claim of the paper. Transcription matches PDF p.28.

Compared Appendix 2 Task 3 definition (divisors add up to exactly 2n) with Mathlib Nat.Perfect (sum properDivisors = n AND 0 < n). The hypothesis 0 < n is needed: with Nat.divisors 0 = empty the paper's formula would hold at 0 while Nat.Perfect 0 is false; the paper's Table 2 says 'positive perfect integer', so excluding 0 matches intent. Status 'known' (Mathlib lemma). Definitional bridge, transcription matches p.28.

Task 3(a) 'If n is perfect, then kn is abundant for any k in N' with N = positive integers, which is the reading the paper itself uses (k = 1 is called the 'limit case', correction is k > 1). Nat.Perfect/Nat.Abundant agree with the paper's all-divisor definitions for n > 0. Disproof (k = 1) is exactly the falsity the paper states on p.9 and Table 2 step [1], so not a straw man; note the paper presents this as a decide-true-or-false task, not as an asserted theorem. Fig. 4 itself is an image I could not extract; wording checked against Appendix 2 only.

Same Task 3(a) text but with k ranging over Lean's N including 0. The paper's handling (k = 1 as the limit case, fix k > 1) indicates N starts at 1, so allowing k = 0 makes this a slightly stronger statement than the paper's; it is literal only under the 0-in-N convention. The statement is false either way (k = 1), so the disproof is not misleading provided the counterexample used is k = 1 rather than k = 0; the _pos variant is the faithful one.

Compared with p.9 ('prompted to provide a proof for k > 1') and Table 2 (n a positive perfect integer, k > 1, conclusion kn abundant). Lean: Nat.Perfect n (includes 0 < n), 1 < k, Nat.Abundant (k*n); via the bridge lemmas this is the paper's all-divisor formulation. No differences found beyond restriction to natural numbers; transcription matches p.9.

Table 2 step [1] 'False for k = 1'. Lean proves the universal form: for every perfect n, 1*n is not abundant, which is the reason the paper's statement fails at k = 1 (slightly more than the bare existence of a counterexample; non-vacuous given ab_perfect_six). Harmless strengthening; transcription matches p.11 (the words 'Limit case' are the Comments column, not part of the step).

Task 3(b) verbatim: 'If p1 and p2 are primes, then p1p2 is abundant'. Lean allows p = q, as the paper's wording does (no distinctness stated); the statement is false in every case so the reading does not matter. Important caveat: Appendix 2 lists this under 'Tasks' as a statement for students to assess, and the paper never asserts it or discusses its truth, so the disproof refutes the literal task text, not a claim the authors make.

Not a claim of the paper: this is the formalizer's own corrected form of Task 3(b); the paper gives no correction and does not discuss the truth of 3(b). The 'original' field quotes the opposite statement from the paper. Mathematically it is the true negation-for-all-primes (p*q has proper divisors summing to at most 1+p+q <= pq), including p = q.

p.17: '6 (the smallest perfect number)' implies 6 is perfect; Lean Nat.Perfect 6 is exactly that under the equivalent proper-divisor definition. Transcription matches PDF page 17 (index 16), sentence spans the page break from p.16.

p.17 names 28 as a perfect number chosen by students, checked by 'sum of their divisors was double the original numbers'. Nat.Perfect 28 is that claim. The 'original' uses an ellipsis joining two adjacent sentences but does not change meaning.

p.17 parenthetical '6 (the smallest perfect number)'. Lean: every perfect n satisfies 6 <= n, which together with ab_perfect_six is exactly minimality; Nat.Perfect excludes 0 so the bound is not broken by n = 0. No differences.
p.19: a student 'found that 8 was not a perfect number'. Lean: not Nat.Perfect 8 (divisors sum 15, not 16). Exact match; it is a reported student finding rather than a theorem of the paper.
Appendix 2 Task 1 'Prove that sqrt 3 + sqrt 5 < 4' vs Real.sqrt 3 + Real.sqrt 5 < 4. Exact match, no differences.

Appendix 2 Task 2(a): f fine iff f(n) = 0 for all n in Z; f, g : R -> R fine implies f + g fine, with (f+g)(x) = f(x)+g(x). Lean inlines the definition of fine and uses pointwise Pi addition, which is the paper's stated meaning. No differences.

Appendix 2 Task 2(b): g(x) = f(x - k) for some k in N, f fine, prove g fine. Lean quantifies universally over k : N (correct reading of 'for some k' in a definition) and inlines fine and g. k = 0 is included in Lean, harmless whichever N convention the paper uses. No other differences.

Appendix 2 Task 4(b). Lean encodes 'preserved in A' as f '' A ⊆ A, reading the paper's 'f(A) ⊂ A' as non-strict inclusion (standard, but a strict reading would give a different statement), and closure of A under multiplication and pointwise product exactly as stated. The paper defines 'preserved' for f : A -> R while 4(b) takes f, g : R -> R; the Lean image formulation handles this. The paper's 'a ⊂ R' typo is transcribed verbatim. Task 4(a) (undefined 'fine set') is not formalized.

Table 2 step [5]: k d_i are among the divisors of kn. Lean: for 0 < k and d in Nat.divisors n (which forces n != 0), k*d in Nat.divisors (k*n). More general than the paper's context (k > 1, n perfect) but implies the step; harmless generalization. Transcription: PDF has 'kdi, kd2, ... kdr' (paper typo), formalizer wrote kd1.
Table 2 step [6]: k d_i != 1 for each i as k > 1. Lean: for all d, 1 < k implies k*d != 1 (d arbitrary natural, not just a divisor) — a harmless generalization. Transcription matches.

Table 2 step [7]: 1 is a divisor of kn. Lean: n perfect, 1 < k implies 1 in Nat.divisors (k*n); the hypotheses are just the proof's context and guarantee kn != 0 (needed because Nat.divisors 0 is empty). No differences.

Table 2 steps [4],[8]: sum of d_i = 2n hence sum of k d_i = 2kn, the d_i being all divisors of perfect n. Lean: for perfect n and any k, sum over Nat.divisors n of k*d = 2*(k*n). Holds for all k rather than only k > 1; harmless. Transcription matches.

Table 2 step [9]. The PDF line reads 'sum of divisors of kn >= sum k d_i = 2kn+1 > sum k d_i = 2kn', which is garbled as printed (a '+1' after the first sum is evidently missing, since step [8] says sum k d_i = 2kn). Lean states the evident intent: 2kn + 1 <= sum of Nat.divisors (k*n) for perfect n, k > 1. Faithful to the intended step, not to the literal (inconsistent) typography; the 'original' reproduces the paper's garbled chain.
Appendix 2 Task 1 'Prove that sqrt 3 + sqrt 5 < 4' vs Real.sqrt 3 + Real.sqrt 5 < 4. Exact match, no differences.

Compared with v3 Sec.1: 'Fibonacci sequence is taken to start at 1, F_1=1, F_2=1' and S_n = sum_{i=1}^n F_i. Lean sums Nat.fib i over Icc 1 n with Nat.fib 1 = Nat.fib 2 = 1. Identical; no differences.

Paper: 'the period with which the sequence of Fibonacci numbers, taken modulo n, repeats' (standard Pisano period, used with Wall's results). Lean: least k>0 with fib(i+k)=fib(i) mod n for all i>=0, which equals the standard definition for n>=1 (pi(1)=1). Only difference is the junk value at n=0, never used.
Paper Remark 3 only says 'L_v is the v-th Lucas number'. Lean 2*fib(n+1)-fib(n) gives 2,1,3,4,7,... = standard L_n; natural subtraction is safe since 2F_{n+1}>=F_n. No differences.

Matches v3 Definition 1 verbatim: F_k | sum_{i=1}^{F_k} F_i. Only difference: Lean k ranges over naturals incl. k=0 (trivially true, 0|0) while paper says 'integer k' and lists terms from 1; immaterial.
Paper Prop 1: 'Let n in N. Then S_n = F_{n+2} - 1.' Lean identical; natural subtraction harmless since fib(n+2)>=1; n=0 also holds (0=0). Checked numerically.

Read v3 HTML myself (and v1, v2: same residues in all three versions). Printed: p>5 prime, S_p = 3 mod p if p=1,4 mod 5; 1 mod p if p=2,3 mod 5, with S_n=F_1+...+F_n, F_1=F_2=1. Lean is the literal statement, not a straw man. Independent Python for all 43 primes 5<p<200: literal reading holds for NO prime (true residues 1 and -2); also false with residues swapped, for S_{p-1}, S_{p+1}, S_{p+2}, sum from F_0, F_{p+2}, or sequence 1,2,3,5. Only the 'in particular p does not divide S_p' sentence is true.

Not a claim of the paper: auditor's corrected residues (1 if p=+-1 mod 5, -2 if p=+-2 mod 5). Verified independently in Python for all primes 5<p<200 and by redoing the paper's Binet computation (k=0 term is C(p+2,1)*5^0=p+2, giving 4F_{p+2}=2+6(5/p)). Informal and source fields do say 'auditor's correction, not the paper's wording', but the origin field is 'paper', which is a mild mislabel.

Matches the last sentence of Theorem 1 ('In particular, S_p is not divisible by p') for primes p>5. True (S_p = 1 or -2 mod p, p>5); checked numerically for p<200. This part of the paper's theorem, and hence its use in the paper, survives.

Paper: self-summable k are those with F_k | (F_{F_k+2} - 1). Lean iff is the same; natural subtraction safe since fib(m+2)>=1. The lists of first terms in the remark are not formalized (not checked by Lean).

Paper: n=2p or 4p, p odd prime, p=2 mod 3, p=+-2 mod 5; then F_n odd and F_{F_n+2}-1 = 0 mod F_n. Lean hypotheses and both conclusions match exactly (p%5=2 or 3 is +-2 mod 5). Checked numerically for p=17,23,47,53, both n. Note on the proof only: for n=4p, F_n = -3 mod 2n (not -1 or 0), so the paper's Eq.(1) is false in that case and one needs F_n+2 = -1 mod 2n with F_{-1}=1; 'a similar argument' needs that modification.

Paper: F_a-F_b = F_u L_v if a=b mod 4, F_v L_u if a=b+2 mod 4, (u,v)=((a-b)/2,(a+b)/2). Lean matches, with integer subtraction on the left; differences: adds hypothesis b<=a and a,b natural (paper leaves range implicit), natural division is exact under the congruence hypotheses. Slight restriction of generality, not a change of meaning.
Paper: n>1, 2|n implies pi(F_n) | 2n. Lean identical using p3_pisano (least positive period). Checked numerically for even n<60 (pi(F_n)=2n for n>=4, pi(F_2)=1).

Paper: lim_{N->inf} min{pi(n)/n : n in N, n<N} = 0. Lean: Tendsto of sInf of the image of Ioo 0 N in the reals; sInf of a finite nonempty set is its min, and n ranges over positive naturals as in the paper (pi(0)/0 is meaningless). Only difference: for N<=1 the set is empty and Lean gives sInf = 0, irrelevant to the limit.

Paper Cor 2: infinitely many odd k with k | sum of first k Fibonacci numbers; Conjecture 1 says 'first n nonzero Fibonacci numbers'. With the paper's convention F_1=1 both are k | S_k, as in Lean. Wording difference (Cor 2 drops 'nonzero') is harmless under the paper's convention; also the paper's proof says both n=2p and n=4p but only uses distinctness of the F_n.
Not a claim of the paper: auxiliary lemma (L_p = 1 and F_p = 5^((p-1)/2) mod p for odd primes) used by the auditor. Standard facts, consistent with my numerics (F_p = +-1 mod p).

Not a claim of the paper: auxiliary lemma (2n is a period of Fibonacci mod F_n for even n), the content of the paper's proof of Proposition 2. Consistent with my check that pi(F_n) | 2n for even n<60.
